quote: Chalmers: I’m perfectly fine. I’ve been introspecting on my consciousness, and I can’t detect any difference. I know I would be expected to say that, but—
content: The joke is a dramatization of the paradox of phenomenal judgment, which Chalmers stated against his own view (The Conscious Mind, ch. 5) and which the previous essays quote him stating. It is a good joke and it is fair to epiphenomenalism. It is not fair to the range of views that accept the zombie argument, since on interactionism and on Russellian monism the zombie Chalmers does not exist (the phenomenal properties are doing the causal work, so removing them changes the physics), and the movie’s premise that “the zombie disease eliminates consciousness without changing the brain in any way” is the epiphenomenalist premise only. The movie is the sequence’s treatment of the alternatives, and the alternatives do not appear in it.

The hero of the film holds a view the sequence disowned the day before. Dennett’s position is that consciousness as ordinarily conceived is a “user illusion,” that there are no qualia in the sense the zombie argument requires, and that the right response to “what is it like?” is to explain why we judge that there is something it is like (Consciousness Explained, 1991; “Quining Qualia,” 1988). That is Type-A materialism, and Zombie Responses declines to accept it (“Type-A materialism is a large bundle; you shouldn’t attribute the bundle to me”), insisting that “what is consciousness?” is a legitimate question demanding “insight” and that the author is “not being eliminative about consciousness.” The sequence wants Dennett’s sword and not Dennett’s conclusion. It is entitled to a third position, and the not-quite-faith-based reductionism of Zombies! Zombies? is one; but the film casts as its champion the philosopher whose actual answer the sequence refused, and “I am one with my body” is not a summary of what either of them believes.
